title: Mbaarih ruht — talking about yesterday
goal: Build past-tense verbs for all eight persons and tell what has already happened.
bekal: add past-tense endings to verbs for all eight persons
use كَان for states in the past

dialogs.title: حَكِي — شُو عْمِلِت مْبَارِح؟
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in class. Laila asks Budi about his weekend, and the story is longer than she expected.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Good morning. What did you do yesterday?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I went to Damascus with Samer.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: shufna el-jaami‘ el-Umawi w mshiina bis-suu’.
lines.id: We saw the Umayyad Mosque and walked around the market.
lines.literal: we-saw the-mosque the-Umayyad and we-walked in-the-market.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: We had falafel. It was really good.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: مِن الصُّبِح لَلْمَغْرِب. تْعِبِت بَسّ اِنْبَسَطِت.
lines.baca: min es-subh la-el-maghrib. ti‘ibt bass inbasaṭ.
lines.id: From morning till sunset. I was tired but happy.
lines.literal: from the-morning till-the-sunset. I-got-tired but I-enjoyed.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: رِكِبْنَا سِرْفِيس. مَا كَان فِي بَاص.
lines.baca: rikibna sirviis. ma kaan fi baaṣ.
lines.id: We took a servees. There was no bus.
lines.literal: we-rode servees. not it-was there-is bus.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: وْسَامِر؟ هُوِّ مَا حَكَى شِي الْيَوْم.
lines.baca: w Saamir? huwwe ma haka shi el-yōm.
lines.id: And Samer? He hasn't said a thing today.
lines.literal: and Samer? he not he-spoke thing today.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: نَام مْتَأَخِّر. مَا فَاق عَ الصَّفّ.
lines.id: He slept late. He didn't get up for class.
lines.literal: he-slept late. not he-got-up for the-class.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Ha ha. And you? Did you study for the exam?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا وَاللَّه، مَا دَرَسِت. رَح إِدْرُس الْيَوْم.
lines.baca: la’ walla, ma darast. rah idrus el-yōm.
lines.id: No, I haven't studied. I'll do it today.
lines.literal: no by-God, not I-studied. will I-study today.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: اَللَّه يْوَفْقَك. أَنَا دَرَسِت مْبَارِح تْلَات سَاعَات.
lines.baca: alla ywaff’ak. ana darast mbaarih tlaat saa‘aat.
lines.id: Good luck. I studied for three hours yesterday.
lines.literal: God may-grant-success. I I-studied yesterday three hours.

notes: **The past tense uses endings, not prefixes.** That's the reverse of the present, which uses the b- prefix. دَرَس ("he studied") becomes دَرَسِت ("I studied") and دَرَسْنَا ("we studied"). The b- prefix **never** appears in the past.
**A verb's dictionary form is the past "he" form.** Look up any verb in any dictionary and you'll find رَاح، أَكَل، دَرَس — not the "I" form. It's also the shortest form and the easiest to remember.

**⚠️ The "I" and "you (m.)" forms are identical.** دَرَسِت can mean "I studied" or "you studied." Add a pronoun when you need to: أَنَا دَرَسِت or إِنْتَ دَرَسِت. In real conversation it's never confusing.

**English often marks time with helpers like "did," "have," or "will"**; Arabic puts it all into the verb itself. There are only two basic shapes — past (endings) and present (prefixes) — so you choose one every time, and "did you…?" or "I have…" need no extra word.

**The word كَان puts a state in the past.** اَلْأَكِل زَاكِي means "the food is good" (now); اَلْأَكِل كَان زَاكِي means "the food was good." It's the only way to put a sentence with no verb into the past.
**The negative is still مَا, with no other change.** The form is مَا دَرَسِت ("I didn't study"). That's simpler than Standard Arabic, which changes the verb form as well.

grammars.title: Past-tense endings
after: ⚠️ Notice how the stem of **رَاح** changes: the long **aa** becomes **u** in every form with a consonant ending — رُحِت، رُحْنَا، رُحْتُوا — but stays **aa** in the "he" and "they" forms: رَاح، رَاحُوا. The same pattern applies to شَاف (شُفِت), نَام (نِمِت), and قَال (قُلِت).
Regular verbs like دَرَس، أَكَل، كَتَب، don't change their stem at all. Just add the ending and you're done.

grammars.title: The verb كَان: states in the past
after: The word كَان can also be paired with a b- verb to express a **past habit**: كِنِت بِدْرُس كِلّ يَوْم ("I used to study every day"). It's the equivalent of English "used to."
Paired with عَم, it means **ongoing in the past**: كِنِت عَم بِدْرُس ("I was studying at the time"). At A1, just recognize and memorize these two combinations without picking apart the rules.

sections.title: The twenty most common past-tense verbs

blocks.text: Verbs ending in ى like حَكَى، قَرَا، عَطَى، اِشْتَرَى change their ending to ـِيت in the "I" form: حْكِيت، قْرِيت، عْطِيت، اِشْتَرِيت. The pattern is regular, so once you get one, you get them all.

blocks.title: Time words for telling the past
items: The most common: مْبَارِح *mbaarih* (yesterday), وَّل مْبَارِح *awwal mbaarih* (the day before yesterday), اَلْأُسْبُوع الْمَاضِي *el-usbuu‘ el-maaḍi* (last week).
For less exact times: قَبِل شْوَي (a while ago), مِن زَمَان (a long time ago), مَرَّة (once).
To stress that it's done: خَلَص *khalaṣ* or خَلَّصِت *khallaṣt* — both mean "done, finished," and the second is only for your own actions.

head: Question
Say it
Meaning
rows: what time did you get there?

blocks.text: The phrase شُو صَار؟ is an all-purpose question meaning both "what happened?" and "so how did it go?" It's used constantly to follow up on something mentioned earlier, and the answer can be as short as مَا صَار شِي ("nothing happened").

blocks.title: Answering when you haven't done it yet
items: The shortest: لِسَّا *lissa* — one word, meaning "not yet," with nothing else needed.
The fuller version: لِسَّا مَا دَرَسِت ("I haven't studied yet"). Notice that لِسَّا and مَا appear together — that's correct.
To promise: رَح إِدْرُس بَعْدَين *rah idrus ba‘dēn* ("I'll study later"). The رَح form is the topic of the next unit.
